I'm reading the Geola website, and it says that...
> Characteristic curves of fine-grain red (PFG-01) and green (VRP-M) emulsions, showing spectral sensitivity versus wavelength, are shown in Fig.1. The VRP-M optical sensitivity (to CW radiation) is seen to peak at approximately 75 mJ/cm2 and that of the PFG-01 (to CW radiation) at approximately 80 mJ/cm2.
 

[http://www.geola.com/holomaterials_vrp_frame.htm](http://www.geola.com/holomaterials_vrp_frame.htm)

Now, the curves are talking about microJoules -- yet the text and exposure table seem to be referring to milliJoules. Is this a misunderstanding, or...?

Anyway, this would seem to indicate that to expose a 4x5 plate with a pulsed laser (60uJ/cm^2 exposure), you'd only need a 3mJ(milliJoule) pulse... right?

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
> **eric343:** Now, the curves are talking about microJoules -- yet the text and exposure table seem to be referring to milliJoules. Is this a misunderstanding, or...?Anyway, this would seem to indicate that to expose a 4x5 plate with a pulsed laser (60uJ/cm^2 exposure), you'd only need a 3mJ(milliJoule) pulse... right?

Text and table error - it should be microJoules, otherwise exposures of at least an hour would be needed with 5 mW lasers, which is thankfully not the case.

4x5 inches (10 x 12.5 cm) is 125 cm^2. Dividing 3 mJ by 125 results in only 24 uJ per cm^2, less than a third of the 75 uJ optimum for VRP.

posts.content_md: Pulsed lasers are a bit tricky with silver. I don't have any experience but I would recomend you read abour repriocity failure and lantensification. The basic idea seems to be that with a very short pulse there is not enough time for the actinic reaction to happen on the surface of the silver grain. Exposing the plate to white light makes the silver grains more active. Someone please correct my errors.

"Pulsed lasers are a bit tricky with silver" as opposed to...? As far as I can tell, you'd need a pretty big laser to do pulsed laser DCG -- at 150mJ/cm^2, 150mJ/cm^2 * 127cm^2 = 19050mJ or **19J!**

Regarding latensification, Geola gives a very nice description of the process:
> PFG-01 and VRP-M emulsions have peak sensitivities to exposures in the millisecond regime. In order to obtain optimal sensitivity to exposures different from this regime the technique of latensification must be used.Latensification is usually done directly after the holographic exposure. Before applying the process a latensification time appropriate for your system must be worked out. This procedure is as follows: Place a 25W white lamp at a distance of 1m from a test holoplate or film such that its light uniformly illuminates the emulsion. You will need to try several exposure times.First of all you will need to develop the unexposed emulsion under normal safelight conditions. The plate will darken a little. This is called the “fog” level. After development wash this control plate, dry and keep it handy. Now a series of exposures with small test plates must be made. Start at about 2 secs and go up to around 10 secs. After each exposure develop your plate and match the darkening of this plate to your control plate. If it is the same, more exposure is needed so go back and repeat the process. Stop when a result that is just marginally darker than the fog level is obtained. This is then the correct latensification exposure for your geometry.Now that the proper latensification time has been discovered, after every proper holoplate exposure you must take your plate and illuminate it exactly as described above for the time that you have worked out. Then all processing is as normal.Latensification stabilizes and enhances the latent image formed by the holographic exposure. If required, chemical processing may be done with significant delay after latensification (~8 hours).

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:0113437273]Latensification stabilizes and enhances the latent image formed by the holographic exposure.[/quote:0113437273]

I suppose you can latensify after exposure or before. I'm not sure why Geola say that latensification causes stability, or in what sense it stabilizes. Presumably they mean that without latensification the latent image would fade. If so, I've never seen anything about latent image fading in pulse holography as opposed to cw holography. I would expect that once the latent image was formed, the means whereby it was formed would not affect any physical parameters. However, the formation of the latent image would have to do with reciprocity, which might indicate pre-latensification. However, it's Geola's film, so I guess they know best.

There's no mention of pulse width in any of the discussions on pulse exposure. The exposure of the plate would depend not only on the energy of the pulse, but also the pulse width.
